Looking for: artists, designers, sound creators and storytellers. Curiosity matters most!
summary:
"Dad, the Internet Went Out" is an educational browser game about space debris and space mission design, created by teenagers  from Capiatá, Paraguay. The player is Dad, a former astronaut who must act when a cascade of space debris destroys the satellites and the internet goes out worldwide. Players use a rocket, choose an orbit, build a ship from parts with mass, cost and power trade-offs, launch, capture junk with the Ñandutí net, land on the Moon and shape one of six endings.

It addresses the Space Mission Design Game challenge by turning real mission engineering into decisions with consequences instead of quizzes. A mission simulator recalculates mass, cost, power, data and lifetime on every change, and every fact comes from open NASA resources such as the Orbital Debris Program Office, Landsat and FIRMS.

It matters because space debris is an invisible threat to the satellites our lives depend on. The game is a single file that runs offline in Spanish and English, so it reaches children with slow connections and old computers.
details:
DAD, THE INTERNET WENT OUT

Team 404 Gravity Not Found - NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

Challenge: Space Mission Design Game

An educational game about space junk, mission design and a family from Capiatá, Paraguay, who decides to save the sky.

MISSION BRIEFING

Every child in the world has said it once: "Dad, the internet went out."

We built a game around that sentence, because it is the most human way we know to explain something huge: the space around our planet is filling with junk, and one day it could switch off the satellites our lives depend on.

20 scenes | 6 endings | 9 songs made by code | 0 engines or libraries

01 - WHY THIS STORY: The threat nobody sees

Capiatá, Paraguay, 2087. Amy is watching TV with her dad when the screen goes black. Not just at home: in the whole country, on the whole planet. A cascade of space debris has destroyed the satellites. No internet, no GPS, no weather forecasts, no calls.

What Amy doesn't know is that her dad, the man who fixes the router and makes chipa on Sundays, was once an astronaut. And he still has a rocket in the garage: the Ñandutí-1, named after the Paraguayan lace that looks like a spider web, the same shape as the net they will use to catch the junk.

We chose space debris because it is the most invisible problem in space. You can't see it from your backyard, but it is already there: tens of thousands of tracked fragments, and far more too small to track, all moving faster than a bullet. Scientists call the worst case the Kessler syndrome: every crash creates more fragments, until some orbits become unusable for generations.

Adults read about this in reports. We wanted a child to feel it, in the moment the cartoon stops and the room goes quiet.

02 - THE JOURNEY: From the sofa to the Moon

The player is Dad. In one play session, a child travels from the family living room to the surface of the Moon. Every stage teaches one piece of how a real space mission works.

1. Living room. The TV goes black. Dad walks the house looking for answers.

2. Garage. Design the ship and pass the test bench.

3. Launch. A real altimeter climbs to the chosen orbit; separate the first stage at 60 km.

4. Orbit. Catch the junk with the Ñandutí net and dodge meteors.

5. Moon landing. Gravity, thrust and fuel: land softly on the green pad.

6. The monster. The trash clumps into a creature. Run, jump and recycle it.

7. On the Moon. Earth looks tiny. Amy asks: "Dad... what do we do now?"

8. Six endings. The TV back on, a junk-covered planet, or something in between.

The exact route depends on the mission chosen: mapping debris, photographing Earth or reaching the Moon. If a ship fails or a stage goes wrong, the player gets up, fixes it and tries again. There are no dead ends, only another attempt.

03 - WHAT A CHILD LEARNS: Decisions, not quizzes

We never wanted a quiz disguised as a game. Every lesson is a decision the player has to make, and the game answers with consequences, not with a grade.

The player decides... and discovers:

- Which rocket to rent: A bigger rocket lifts more but costs more coins. Every mission is a budget.

- Which orbit to fly to: Low orbit (400 km) is cheap and close; geostationary orbit (36,000 km) sees a whole hemisphere but is far away.

- Which parts to build in: Solar panels, batteries, antennas, a shield, a net, a robotic arm, fuel tanks. Every part adds mass, cost and power demand.

- Whether the ship passes the tests: Too heavy, and it won't lift off. Weak antennas, and the science never reaches Earth.

- How to catch the zombie satellite: Space junk spins; you must slow it down before you can grab it.

- How to land on the Moon: Gravity is six times weaker there, but it still pulls. Too fast and you crash.

- What to do at the end: Amy's last question changes the ending. Real missions are also about choices.

This is how real space engineers work: trade-offs between mass, cost, power, data and lifetime. We simplified the numbers, not the thinking.

When a child fails, the game doesn't just say "Game Over". Amy and Dad talk about what went wrong and what it means for the people back on Earth. Failure becomes a conversation, not a punishment.

04 - BUILT BY HAND: Line by line, from scratch

No game engine. No libraries. No audio files. Pure JavaScript drawn on an HTML5 canvas, in a single file of about 280 KB that opens in any browser, on a cheap phone or an old school computer. We chose the hard road on purpose: a game about the internet going out had to work when the internet goes out.

System - What we built:

- Game loop and scenes: 20 scenes connected with fades, each with its own music

- Dialogue engine: Speaker, emotion, typewriter text, choices that branch the story

- Mission simulator: Recalculates mass, cost, power, data, science and lifetime on every change

- Physics: Ascent with altimeter, stage separation, lunar gravity, a spinning satellite

- Pathfinding: Dad walks around the furniture to wherever the child taps

- Music: 9 songs composed in real time with the Web Audio API

- Translation: Full Spanish and English, including sentences with changing numbers

- Testing: A "robot player" that plays the whole story end to end to catch bugs

We are 15 and 17 years old, and we spent hours and hours on every one of these systems, rewriting them until they felt right in a child's hands.

05 - DESIGNED WITH LOVE: Home first, then space

- A real Paraguayan house: the sofa, the TV and the router blinking on the shelf.

- Characters drawn in eight directions. Dad, Amy and their dog turn to face wherever they walk. Amy picks her space suit from seven colors; Dad always wears his old one.

- Faces that feel. Every line of dialogue carries an emotion: surprise, doubt, a tear, a blush, a spark of joy.

- Our culture in orbit. The rocket is named Ñandutí, the lace of Itauguá. Chipa, the bread of every Paraguayan family, heals you during the mission.

- Music for every moment: calm at home, adventurous in the garage, epic at launch, tense in the chase, soft on the Moon.

- Two languages, completely. In English, everything is in English: menus, jokes, facts, even the title logo.

- Six endings. The best is the simplest: Amy and Dad back on the sofa, the TV on. The worst shows the planet buried in junk.

Nothing here came from a template. Every background, sprite sheet and portrait was made, cut, aligned and tuned by us until it looked right.

06 - NASA AT THE CORE: Every fact has a source

Every fact a child reads in the game comes from open NASA resources, credited on the game's own "NASA Data" screen. The science stage turns them into gameplay: the player photographs Earth, maps debris or studies the Moon.

- Orbital Debris Program Office: The whole premise: how much junk is up there, how it is tracked, and the Kessler syndrome. (orbitaldebris.jsc.nasa.gov)

- Landsat (NASA and USGS): Photographing the Paraguay River: Earth imaged since 1972 to watch rivers and forests change. (landsat.gsfc.nasa.gov)

- NASA FIRMS: Photographing the Chaco forest: satellites mapping fires in near real time to warn people. (firms.modaps.eosdis.nasa.gov)

- NASA Black Marble: Asunción at night: maps of Earth's lights, and of where the lights go out. (blackmarble.gsfc.nasa.gov)

- International Space Station: Low orbit at about 400 km, orbital speed and Earth's shadow. (nasa.gov/international-space-station)

- Apollo and lunar missions: Moon rocks, footprints, ice in dark craters and gravity six times weaker. (nasa.gov/humans-in-space/apollo)

Satellites are not a luxury. They warn us about fires and hurricanes, show us melting ice, and connect a family in Capiatá with the rest of the world. Protecting the space around Earth is protecting life on Earth.

07 - THE IMPACT WE WANT: Made for the kids who need it most

Most children in the world will never visit a space agency. Many of them, in Paraguay and across Latin America, go to schools with slow connections and old computers. This game was made for them first.

- It reaches anyone with a link: One file. No installation, no account, no store. It runs on phones, tablets and old laptops, and keeps running offline once open.

- It speaks their language: Spanish and English, with local words, local food and a local house. A child learns more when they see themselves in the story.

- A global problem, a family problem: Space debris stops being a statistic and becomes: "my cartoon stopped, and my dad has to go fix it."

- It plants a real idea: The sky is not infinite, and what we leave up there stays. This generation will decide how we use orbit.

- It brings families together: The game is about a father and a daughter. We hope it starts the same conversation at real kitchen tables.

If one child closes this game, looks up at the night sky and thinks "someone has to take care of that, and it could be me," then every hour we spent was worth it.

08 - FROM OUR TEAM: 404 Gravity Not Found

We are not a studio. We are just teenagers from Paraguay, learning as we built. We stayed up late, broke the game a hundred times and fixed it a hundred and one.

We redrew the characters when they didn't look like us. We rewrote the physics when the landing felt unfair. We translated every sentence because a child in another country deserved the same game.

We put into this project the same thing Dad puts into the Ñandutí-1: everything we had, out of love for the people waiting at home.

The internet can go out. Curiosity doesn't have to.

- Team 404 Gravity Not Found, Capiatá, Paraguay
